definition: Robot-sumo (Japanese: ロボット相撲) is an engineering and robotics competition in which two robots attempt to push each other out of a circular arena, in a similar fashion to the sport of sumo.
details: The robots used in this competition are called "sumo robots", "sumobots" or simply "sumos". Competitions typically involve autonomously operated wheeled mobile robots. The engineering challenges are for the robot to find its opponent (usually accomplished with infrared or ultra-sonic sensors) and to push it out of the dohyō. A robot should also avoid leaving the arena, usually by means of a sensor that detects the edge. The most common mechanical design is to use a wedge with a blade at the front to lift the opposing robot and push it more easily. Robot-Sumo originated in Japan in 1989 when FUJISOFT Inc. [jp] organized an experimental robot-sumo tournament, which would later be established as the All Japan Robot Sumo Tournament [jp](Japanese: 全日本ロボット相撲大会 zen'nippon robotto sumou taikai). Since 1998, FUJISOFT has collaborated with more than 30 countries, and robot-sumo has spread and has been one of the most popular robotics competitions in the world, such as in Europe, Mexico and Brazil, with a total of 80,000 people around the world actively developing sumo robots. explainer.lead: Robot-sumo is a competition where two robots try to push each other out of a circular arena, much like human sumo. It matters as a compact engineering testbed for sensing, control and mechanical design.

tiers.eli5: Two little robots face off in a round ring and try to shove each other out, like sumo wrestlers, but built by engineers.
tiers.practitioner: Most entries are autonomous wheeled robots that find the opponent using infrared or ultrasonic sensors and detect the arena edge to avoid driving out. The usual pitfall is the robot leaving the ring itself while chasing.
tiers.paperLevel: The task is constrained to a circular arena (dohyo): locate the opponent, push it out, and avoid crossing the boundary, typically relying on edge-detection sensing. Success depends on sensor coverage and pushing design rather than formal optimality.

explainer.example: A wedge-shaped sumobot with a front blade uses edge sensors to stop at the ring boundary while its opponent sensor steers it into the other robot.
